analysis.one_liner: Pays workers 55% of wages for 12 weeks of family or medical leave, funded by a small employer payroll tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in two House committees and a subcommittee until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a national family and medical leave insurance program paying eligible workers 55% of their weekly earnings for up to 12 weeks of leave to care for a newborn or adopted child, recover from a serious illness, or care for a sick family member. It would be financed by a 0.4% payroll tax on employers, with employers that already offer an equivalent or better plan exempt from the tax. Self-employed workers could opt in, and employers could not fire or penalize workers for taking the leave. It never got past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who need time off for childbirth, adoption, their own serious illness, or a sick family member, and who today often cannot afford unpaid leave. Eligibility is broad: a worker qualifies with as little as $250 in earnings per quarter, and the bill lowers the covered-employer threshold from 50 employees to 1, so workers at very small businesses are covered — unlike under current family leave law. Self-employed people could choose to pay the tax and receive benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers who cannot afford unpaid leave

how_it_helps.text: Provides an entitlement to 12 workweeks of paid leave at 55% of weekly earnings (capped at $1,350 per week for 2008) for birth or adoption of a child, a serious health condition, or care for a child, parent, spouse, or household member with a serious medical condition.

Covers far more workers than existing unpaid leave law: the bill redefines a covered employer as one with a single employee, and makes any worker who earned at least $250 in each of the prior four quarters eligible, including self-employed people who elect to participate.
Makes it unlawful for employers to interfere with or deny leave rights or to fire or discriminate against workers who use them, with damages, reinstatement, and attorney's fees available in court.

analysis.who_pays: Employers pay a 0.4% payroll tax on wages to fund the trust fund — and under the bill's definition, that applies to every employer with even one employee, from the largest firm down to a household employer. Employers can avoid the tax by offering a Labor Department-approved voluntary plan that is as good as or better than the public program. Some economists would note that payroll taxes can be partly passed to workers through lower wages.

drawbacks.text: The 0.4% payroll tax applies to every employer with even one employee, a real cost for the smallest businesses even though the amount is modest compared with the existing 6.2% Social Security payroll tax.

The benefit is partial: it replaces only 55% of wages, is capped at $1,350 per week, and pays nothing during a 7-day waiting period at the start of each leave — so a worker taking a short leave could receive little or nothing.
Benefits are offset by other sources for the same period, including workers' compensation, unemployment insurance, and approved employer plans, so workers with those benefits see no added income.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary workers the benefit is substantial: paid time for the events — a new baby, cancer treatment, an aging parent — that otherwise force people to quit or go into debt. The cost side is real but modest: a 0.4% employer payroll tax with an exemption for employers who already provide equivalent coverage, and a benefits structure that is deliberately lean (55% replacement, a one-week unpaid wait, a weekly cap). An honest supporter would acknowledge the tax reaches the smallest employers and that partial wage replacement still leaves gaps; the design's bigger weakness is that it launched with no bipartisan support, giving it no realistic path.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, then sent to a subcommittee in May 2006; neither committee ever acted, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the Paid Family and Medical Leave Act of 2005 in the House on June 30, 2005, joined by four original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to both the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.

On May 1, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — its last recorded action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history before the 109th Congress ended January 3, 2007.
The bill gathered 28 cosponsors, all of them Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off because the bill died: no 0.4% payroll tax was enacted. Workers who lack paid leave gained nothing; the United States still had no federal paid family and medical leave program.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided the payroll tax

sides.party_line_note: All 29 named supporters — the sponsor and 28 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored; there were no recorded votes, and the Republican-controlled committees took no action.

industries.note: Employers would owe a new 0.4% payroll tax on wages, though employers with a Labor-Department-approved plan equal to or better than the program are exempt. The bill itself argued businesses benefit through retention and productivity, but the direct fiscal effect is a new tax.

Employers can escape the payroll tax by offering a voluntary plan, but such a plan must provide insurance issued by an approved admitted disability insurer — creating a new private insurance market alongside the public program.
The bill lowers the covered-employer threshold from 50 employees to 1, so even a one-employee business would owe the payroll tax, a cost existing family leave law never imposed on them.
